_about: College batch 10: junior year (COL_080-083, 085, 088, 094-096, 099-102). Continues the family chain ({parent}'s Health Scare) and adds two wrong-path strikes (online_incident, rode_along).

scenarios.title: The Old Injury Returns
scenarios.text: The groin strain is back, worse this time, right before the conference schedule. The trainer wants two weeks of rehab, and you can feel it on every kickoff.

choices.label: Do the full two weeks
choices.result: You do every band, every ice bath and every boring stretch for two weeks. It's slow and maddening, and the strain is gone when it's over.

choices.label: Rehab and kick short
choices.result: You rehab in the mornings and kick only short field goals in practice. You keep your timing, and the strain stays exactly where it was.

choices.label: Tape it and keep going
choices.result: You tape it, take the full load and say nothing. The leg holds for now, and it hurts more every week.

choices.label: Tell them everything this time
choices.result: You hid an injury once and paid for it. This time you tell the trainer everything, including the parts you'd usually leave out, and the plan fits exactly what's wrong.

scenarios.title: A High School Teammate Calls
scenarios.text: Someone from your old high school team calls: they're visiting campus next weekend for a college visit and need a place to stay and a tour.

choices.label: Host them all weekend
choices.result: You give up your bed, show them every corner of campus and introduce them to half the team. They leave saying they want to come here.

choices.label: Give them one good afternoon
choices.result: You give the tour on Saturday, buy lunch and point them to a hotel. It's friendly, and you keep your weekend.

choices.label: Say it's a bad weekend
choices.result: You say it's a bad weekend, which is true. They understand, and you feel a little bad about it.

choices.label: Give them the visit you wish you'd had
choices.result: You helped a freshman find their way in high school, so you plan the visit you wish you'd had: real questions, honest answers, no sales pitch.
choices.lock_text: having helped a younger player find their way before

scenarios.title: Trouble at Home
scenarios.text: {sibling} got suspended from school for a fight. {parent} calls, overwhelmed, and asks you to talk to him.

choices.label: Call {sibling} that night
choices.result: You call and mostly listen. It turns out the fight was about someone saying something about {parent}. You don't excuse it, and you don't lecture.

choices.label: Give him a hard talk
choices.result: You tell {sibling} he's better than this and there's no excuse. He goes quiet and says 'okay' too fast.

choices.label: Invite him up for a weekend
choices.result: You ask {parent} to send {sibling} to campus for the weekend. You take him to practice and let the linemen talk to him, which works better than anything you could say.

scenarios.title: {parent}'s Health Scare
scenarios.text: A late-night call: {parent} is in the hospital. They think it's his heart. You're four hundred miles away, and there's a game on Saturday.

choices.label: Go home now
choices.result: You tell {coach} and take the first flight out. You sit with {parent} for two days, fly back Friday night and barely sleep before the game.

choices.label: Stay and call every hour
choices.result: {sibling} is there, and {parent} insists you stay. You call every few hours and stare at your phone through every meeting.

choices.label: Ask {coach} what to do
choices.result: You go to {coach}'s office at midnight. The coach says family first and books the flight before you can argue.

choices.label: Ask {parent} what he needs
choices.result: You ask {parent}, plainly, whether he wants you there. He says yes, which he's never said before. You're on the plane by morning.
choices.lock_text: having learned to talk openly with your family

scenarios.title: Choosing a Major
scenarios.text: You have to declare a major by Friday. One keeps you eligible with the least effort; another is the one you actually care about and comes with a lab that meets during practice twice a month.

choices.label: Pick the one you care about
choices.result: You declare the hard major and work out the lab schedule with {teacher} and {coach}. It's harder every semester, and it's yours.

choices.label: Pick the easy one
choices.result: You declare the major that keeps you eligible with room to spare. Your schedule gets easier, and your classes get boring.

choices.label: Ask {teacher} for a third option
choices.result: You ask {teacher} whether there's something in between. There is: a minor in what you care about, on top of the easier major.

choices.label: Follow the plan you made years ago
choices.result: You planned this in high school, so you declare the hard major and hand {teacher} a four-semester schedule that already works around practice. It leaves no room for anything fun.
choices.lock_text: having planned your academic path in high school

scenarios.title: The Viral Video
scenarios.text: A teammate posts a video of you at a party, edited to make you look much worse than you were. It's everywhere by morning, with your name in the caption.

choices.label: Go to the media staff first
choices.result: You send the video and the original to the team's media staff before practice. They get it taken down and ask the teammate to post an apology.

choices.label: Talk to the teammate
choices.result: You find him at lunch and ask him to take it down. He does, sheepishly. The screenshots are still out there.

choices.label: Fire back online
choices.result: You post your own video calling him out by name, with a few things he wouldn't want public. By lunch, you're both in {coach}'s office, and the story is twice as big.

scenarios.title: The Watch List
scenarios.text: You make a preseason watch list for the best kicker in the country. Your phone won't stop: reporters, old coaches, a cousin you haven't heard from in six years.

choices.label: Answer everyone
choices.result: You answer every text and call back every reporter. It's a great week and a long one.

choices.label: Turn the phone off for a day
choices.result: You thank people in one post and turn the phone off for a day. When it's back on, the world has moved on to someone else.

choices.label: Give the credit away
choices.result: In every interview you talk about {holder}, the snapper and {coach}. The specialists' group chat is very happy.

scenarios.title: The Conference Title Race
scenarios.text: Your team is in the conference title race, and the campus has lost its mind. Everyone wants a piece of the players this week: interviews, photos, parties, a pep rally.

choices.label: Say yes to the pep rally only
choices.result: You go to the pep rally, say a few words and leave the rest. The students chant your name for a full minute.

choices.label: Go into lockdown
choices.result: You go to class, practice and bed. Nothing else. It's boring, and you've never felt more ready.

choices.label: Take the younger players' calls
choices.result: You become the person the freshmen call when the attention gets too much. You spend the week calming other people down.

scenarios.title: The Holder's Senior Day
scenarios.text: It's {holder}'s last home game, and {holder} asks you to walk out with their family on senior day.

choices.label: Walk out with them
choices.result: You walk out with {holder}'s family, and their grandmother holds your arm the whole way. {holder} doesn't stop smiling.

choices.label: Write {holder} a letter instead
choices.result: You say you'd rather give {holder} the moment with family and hand over a letter about three years of holds. {holder} reads it in the training room and goes very quiet.

choices.label: Say yes, then get back to warming up
choices.result: You walk out, hug everyone at midfield and jog straight to the net. {holder} laughs about it later. Mostly.

scenarios.title: A Teammate Enters the Portal
scenarios.text: Your closest friend on the team enters the transfer portal without telling you first. You find out from a reporter's post.

choices.label: Call him and ask why
choices.result: You call that night. He says he couldn't tell you because you'd talk him out of it. You don't try to, and the friendship survives.

choices.label: Let it hurt for a while
choices.result: You don't call. It stings for weeks, and you throw yourself into the summer program.

choices.label: Help him find the right place
choices.result: You help him think through the offers and call a coach you know at one of the schools. He lands somewhere good, and sends you a photo from the first practice.

scenarios.title: The Late-Night Drive
scenarios.text: After curfew, a teammate who's in no shape to drive grabs his keys and says everyone's going for food. Three guys are already heading for the car.

choices.label: Take the keys
choices.result: You take the keys out of his hand and call for a ride. He's angry for the rest of the night and thanks you on Monday.

choices.label: Stay behind and order in
choices.result: You say you're staying and order pizza for whoever stays with you. Two of the guys stay. The other two go.

choices.label: Get in the car
choices.result: You get in the back seat. A campus officer pulls the car over two blocks later, and by morning every name in it is on {coach}'s desk.

scenarios.title: Academic Honors
scenarios.text: {teacher} says you're close to academic all-conference, if you take one more hard class this semester instead of an easy elective.

choices.label: Take the hard class
choices.result: You take the hard class and spend Sundays in the library. The honor comes in December, and {teacher} frames the letter for the office wall.

choices.label: Take the easy elective
choices.result: You take the easy class and keep your Sundays free. The honor goes to someone else, and you get two more hours of sleep a week.

choices.label: Ask a teammate to take it with you
choices.result: You talk a teammate into taking the hard class with you, and you study together every Sunday. You both make it.

choices.label: Do what you've always done
choices.result: You've never taken the easy class, and you're not starting now. You sign up for the hard one and make a study schedule before you leave the office. Sundays are gone.
choices.lock_text: having put real effort into school before

scenarios.title: The Weight Room Push
scenarios.text: The new strength coach wants you to add power fast. Your legs are already sore, and his program doesn't believe in rest days.

choices.label: Do the whole program
choices.result: You do every set, every day. Your legs feel like concrete by June, and by August they're stronger than they've ever been.

choices.label: Ask for a kicker's version
choices.result: You ask him for a version with rest days built in for specialists. He grumbles and writes one, and the punter thanks you.

choices.label: Quietly do less
choices.result: You skip the sets you think are too much and don't mention it. Your legs feel good. The strength coach notices the numbers.

choices.label: Show him your plan
choices.result: You bring him the training plan you've kept since high school and ask him to build on it. He's impressed, and the result fits you.
choices.lock_text: having built your own training plan before
